explanation: Beck, an engineering draughtsman, drew lines only vertical, horizontal or at 45 degrees and spaced stations more evenly. The Thames was the one natural feature he kept.

claims.text: Harry Beck's London Underground diagram, published in 1933, ignored true geographical distances between stations.
Beck's 1933 map kept the River Thames, the station names and coloured lines.
Harry Beck was an engineering draughtsman.
Beck drew lines only vertically, horizontally or at 45 degrees, and spaced stations more evenly than a geographic map would.
The River Thames was the only natural feature shown on Beck's map.

Mapping London: the iconic Tube map
Original sketch for the London Underground Railways Map

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Not to scale: The map showed relationships rather than distances. Beck drew on electrical schematics, so showing only the relationships and not the distances between various points. Publication: The design was first drafted in 1931, rejected at first, and printed as a pocket map in 1933 (He presented his original draft in 1931, and after initial rejection it was first printed in 1933.).

claimResults.note: London Transport Museum (which holds the 1933 pocket maps), the Design Museum and Wikipedia: Beck's diagram, first printed in 1933, showed how stations connect rather than the distances between them.

evidence.query: Beck January 1933 pocket Underground map shows River Thames in blue, the only geographical feature, coloured lines and station names

results.title: Map; Pocket Underground map, by Henry C Beck, January 1933
Transforming the Tube map: Harry Beck’s iconic design
Mapping London: the iconic Tube map
Original sketch for the London Underground Railways Map

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Coloured lines: Design Museum notes say Beck represented each line in a different colour and interchange stations as diamonds. Station names: Museum of London commentary says Beck made some alterations, in particular making station names more prominent before the pocket version. River Thames: Wikipedia says Beck's simplified design included stations, straight-line segments connecting them, and the River Thames. None of the results say the river was drawn in blue or that it was the only geographical feature, so I couldn't verify those two details.

claimResults.note: Answers checker B's ambiguity issue: Wikipedia, named in the summary, lists the River Thames in Beck's simplified design; the Design Museum says each line had its own colour; the London Transport Museum record of the January 1933 pocket edition mentions the station names. The Thames was kept, so 'The River Thames' is not a second answer to 'dropping what?'.
